newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN's enlargement may challenge consensus.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN's enlargement may challenge consensus.

text.p: The admission of new members into the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) may challenge the group's cherished system of decision-making by consensus, Malaysia's foreign minister said on Monday.

"It would not surprise me if in the immediate years ahead one of the major challenges that confront us will be maintaining cohesion and preserving consensus in the face of a near-doubling in ASEAN membership within the short span of just two or three years," Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi said.

Speaking at an ASEAN Congress of diplomats, academics and businessmen, Abdullah said: "ASEAN five and ASEAN six were already diverse in terms of political systems, economic levels and strategic outlooks. ASEAN nine and ASEAN 10 will be even Malaysia is this year's chairman of ASEAN, which is holding its annual series of meetings in Kuala Lumpur beginning on Wednesday. Senior officials from ASEAN -- Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- began talks on Monday to prepare the agenda.
Burma and Laos will be admitted as ASEAN's eighth and ninth members on Wednesday. Cambodia's induction has been postponed because of the political turmoil there.
"I see this as a temporary setback," Abdullah said. "I look forward to Cambodia joining the group in the near future once the problems are resolved."

ASEAN was founded 30 years ago at the height of the Vietnam War, when insurgency was rife throughout a region that had become a Cold War battleground, and today's booming economies were mostly mired in poverty.
Recalling those years, Abdullah said: "Every state, without exception, was suspicious of its neighbours and relations were acutely strained in the case of some.
"There are no longer two contending parts, one communist and the other non-communist."
But he added it was critically important for ASEAN to nurture and reinforce its identity, cohesion and vitality as the group expanded.
Consensus-building would be more difficult and ASEAN may have to allow dissenting countries to opt out of the group's common positions, a formula known as "ASEAN minus X", he said.

Resolving conflicting territorial claims would remain ASEAN's most vexing issue, Abdullah said. "We look to a Southeast Asia that has resolved all territorial disputes and all border politics by the year 2020."

Narcotics trafficking "will become an important item in ASEAN's agenda as it expands", he added. New members Burma and Laos form, along with northern Thailand, the infamous "Golden Triangle" poppy-growing area for heroin production.
"Southeast Asia must work very hard to cease having the dubious distinction of being the world's largest producer of drugs," Abdullah said.
Piracy in some of the world's busiest sea lanes was another scourge the group was trying to tackle, he said.
"Our waters are fertile pickings for pirates. Here, too, Southeast Asia and East Asia enjoy the unfortunate reputation of having the largest number of incidents of piracy in the world."
